title: Subsets
summary: Generate every subset. At each recursion level, record the current path as a subset, then try extending it with each remaining element after `start`. Undo the choice after recursing. Using only later elements avoids duplicates like [2, 1].

complexity.note: 2ⁿ subsets, each copied in O(n). Recursion depth n.

intuition: Every node of the recursion tree is a subset, so add the path on entry.
`start` ensures elements are picked in increasing index order.
Add, recurse, remove: the path is restored for the next choice.
Bitmasks from 0 to 2ⁿ−1 are an iterative alternative.
pitfalls: Adding `path` itself instead of a copy: every result ends up empty.
Starting the loop at 0 instead of `start` creates duplicates.

edgeCases.name: Empty input
edgeCases.why: The empty set is still a subset.

title: Permutations

complexity.note: n! permutations, each copied in O(n).

intuition: A boolean `used[]` array tracks which numbers are already in the path.
When the path has n numbers, it's a complete permutation.
Unmark after recursing so later branches can use the number.
pitfalls: Using `path.contains(x)` to check usage is O(n) per check.
Forgetting to copy the path when saving it.

Python.code:
def permute(nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
    res, used = [], [False] * len(nums)

    def dfs(path: List[int]) -> None:
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            if used[i]: continue
            used[i] = True
            path.append(nums[i])
            dfs(path)
            path.pop()
            used[i] = False

    dfs([])
    return res

title: Combination Sum
summary: Find all combinations of candidates (each usable any number of times) that sum to `target`. Sort, then recurse with a remaining target. Passing the same index `i` again allows reuse; stopping when a candidate exceeds the remainder prunes the search.

complexity.note: T = target, m = smallest candidate (bounds the depth).

intuition: Recurse with `i` (not `i + 1`) to allow picking the same number again.
Starting each loop at `start` keeps combinations in non-decreasing order, so no duplicates.
After sorting, once a candidate is too big, every later one is too, so break.
pitfalls: Looping from 0 produces [2, 3, 2] and [3, 2, 2] as different results.

def combinationSum2(candidates: List[int], target: int) -> List[List[int]]:
    candidates.sort()
    res = []

    def find(start: int, remain: int, path: List[int]) -> None:
        if remain == 0:
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        for i in range(start, len(candidates)):
            if i > start and candidates[i] == candidates[i - 1]: continue
            if candidates[i] > remain: break
            path.append(candidates[i])
            find(i + 1, remain - candidates[i], path)
            path.pop()

    find(0, target, [])
    return res

title: Word Search
summary: Does the word exist as a path of adjacent cells, using each cell at most once? Try every starting cell. DFS matches one letter at a time, temporarily marking the cell as used, and unmarks it on the way back.

complexity.note: L = word length. Each step has at most 3 new directions.

intuition: A cell can be reused in a different path, but not twice in the same path.
Mark in place (e.g. '#') instead of a separate visited array.
Restore the letter after exploring: that's the backtracking step.
Stop as soon as one path matches.
pitfalls: Checking `index == word.length()` after the bounds check instead of before.

def exist(board: List[List[str]], word: str) -> bool:
    m, n = len(board), len(board[0])

    def match(k: int, r: int, c: int) -> bool:
        if k == len(word): return True
        if r < 0 or c < 0 or r >= m or c >= n or board[r][c] != word[k]: return False
        saved = board[r][c]
        board[r][c] = '#'
        found = (match(k + 1, r + 1, c) or match(k + 1, r - 1, c)
                 or match(k + 1, r, c + 1) or match(k + 1, r, c - 1))
        board[r][c] = saved
        return found

    return any(match(0, r, c) for r in range(m) for c in range(n))

title: Palindrome Partitioning
summary: Split a string into pieces that are all palindromes, returning every way. From position `start`, try each end `i`; if `s[start..i]` is a palindrome, take it and recurse on the rest. Reaching the end means one full partition.

complexity.note: Up to 2ⁿ⁻¹ partitions; each palindrome check is O(n).

intuition: Each recursion level chooses the next cut.
Only palindromic prefixes are worth exploring.
Precomputing a palindrome table makes each check O(1).
pitfalls: Forgetting to copy the path into the result.

title: N-Queens
summary: Place n queens so none attack each other. Place one queen per row; for each row try every column not under attack. Three sets track used columns and both diagonals (`r - c` and `r + c`), so checking a square is O(1).

complexity.note: At most n choices in the first row, n−1 in the next, and so on.

intuition: One queen per row, so recursion depth is n.
Squares on the same ↘ diagonal share `r - c`; on the same ↙ diagonal they share `r + c`.
Add to the sets before recursing, remove after.
pitfalls: Checking the whole board for every placement is O(n) per check.
Forgetting one of the two diagonals.

def solveNQueens(n: int) -> List[List[str]]:
    res, queens = [], [0] * n
    cols, diag, anti = set(), set(), set()

    def place(r: int) -> None:
        if r == n:
            res.append(["." * c + "Q" + "." * (n - c - 1) for c in queens])
            return
        for c in range(n):
            if c in cols or r - c in diag or r + c in anti: continue
            queens[r] = c
            cols.add(c); diag.add(r - c); anti.add(r + c)
            place(r + 1)
            cols.remove(c); diag.remove(r - c); anti.remove(r + c)

    place(0)
    return res
